title: KDE turns 30 with Plasma 6.8, remote upgrades, and an X11 farewell
gist: KDE marked its 30th anniversary on October 14 with Plasma 6.8, which drops native X11 session support in favor of Wayland (X11 apps still run via XWayland), and adds remote desktop, CPU pinning and other features. A documentary was also released.

themes.theme: X11 session support ends in Plasma

insights.claim: Plasma 6.8 retires support for starting new native X11 sessions and fully adopts Wayland, while legacy X11 apps keep working through XWayland and KDE applications continue supporting X11 under other desktop environments.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Linux desktop is consolidating on Wayland; X11-dependent workflows need XWayland or an older release.

insights.claim: Users staying on Plasma 6.7 keep their existing X11 sessions for now, giving a temporary migration path.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Defines the migration window for X11-dependent users.

insights.claim: KDE's X11 exit was expected, since GNOME officially dropped X11 sessions by default in 2025, so the 42-year-old X11 protocol is losing another major desktop environment.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Both major Linux desktops are off X11, which reduces the incentive to maintain X11-only software.

insights.claim: Plasma 6.8 adds window decorations such as shadows and rounded corners for third-party apps, a more streamlined Union theming system, Nvidia triple buffering by default, Kup backup integration and the kscreenctl command-line tool for display configuration.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Enabling Nvidia triple buffering by default signals continued work on Nvidia support under Wayland.
insights.locator: The new Plasma 6.8 brings many improvements

insights.claim: The revamped System Monitor lets users pin processes to specific CPU cores through a GUI.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Power-user tuning previously done by command line is now exposed in the GUI.

insights.claim: KDE rebuilt Plasma's built-in remote desktop server for clients accessing virtual displays over a network, adding clipboard synchronization, an Exclusive Mode that locks the physical display while the client sets a matching virtual one, and adaptive streaming for slower networks.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Makes Plasma more viable as a self-hosted remote workstation, a niche of the homelab segment.
insights.locator: Homelabbers should find plenty to be excited about

insights.claim: KDE released The KDE Documentary - A Story of Free Software Underdogs alongside Plasma 6.8 for its 30th anniversary.
insights.speaker: Nick Indge
insights.so_what: Marketing and community milestone with no direct financial implication.
insights.locator: Linux enthusiasts can also check out a new movie
